assumptions: Qualified partners can lawfully retain responsibility for testing, waste-status assessment, warehousing, transport, and installation under contracts that clearly bound the desk's product-liability exposure.
A subset of obsolete off-warranty inverter and optimizer failures carries enough avoided repowering cost to support a meaningful outcome fee.
Installers and partners will permit the desk to retain sufficiently detailed, lawful case and outcome data to build the proposed fitment graph.
The family installer's cases provide useful initial access, but are not assumed to prove broader Polish demand or representative economics.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A prospective cohort of Polish installers should provide case logs showing the annual failure count, the share still unresolved after OEM and SecondSol searches, documented avoided-repowering cost, quoted customer fees, paid conversion, resolution rate, full contribution after testing/returns/warranty/insurance/support, repeat frequency, and retention; this should be paired with signed qualified-partner terms covering supply, testing, service levels, non-waste documentation, fitment responsibility, and liability.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The residual-case framing is disciplined: value may exist where obsolete off-warranty electronics cannot be straightforwardly replaced and documented compatibility avoids repowering. The insight is plausible, but the packet does not establish that this residual pool is frequent or valuable enough to form a business.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: A failed inverter or optimizer can create urgent downtime and an expensive repowering alternative, so pain can be acute in qualifying cases. However, willingness to pay, avoided cost, paid resolution rate, and repeat frequency are all unvalidated, while OEMs and SecondSol may resolve many attractive cases.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Using existing channels, avoiding inventory, and charging on successful outcomes limit initial capital exposure. The model nevertheless lacks evidence for price, gross contribution, resolution rate, CAC, payback, retention, cash conversion, guarantee costs, or owner earnings, and it earns primarily on unusually difficult cases with potentially high variable costs.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Polish installers with obsolete off-warranty inverter and optimizer failures form a coherent, reachable beachhead against a large installed microinstallation base. Its economically relevant size is unknown because the evidence does not quantify failures by model or the share left unresolved by OEM and incumbent channels.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Local language, managed case handling, and closed-loop fitment records could support a focused Polish service position. Yet SecondSol already supplies a closely matching European stack at scale, OEM replacement removes easier demand, and the desk presently controls neither unique supply nor exclusive installer distribution.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A proven case graph and installer-account workflow could extend to adjacent PV components, maintenance decisions, additional installers, and nearby geographies. Expansion remains conditional on first proving that the narrow residual wedge has repeatable economics, and geographic expansion would increase regulatory, supply, and compatibility complexity.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Serial-level test, context, fitment, and verified-outcome data could improve routing and compatibility decisions over time. That moat starts empty, depends on partners and installers contributing outcomes, may accumulate slowly because failures are fragmented, and could be replicated by a larger marketplace or OEM-linked service.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Outcome-contingent managed procurement and documented fitment could save installer time and avoid full repowering in the narrow cases it solves. The packet gives no comparative evidence on resolution speed, success, price, trust, or total savings versus an installer's own OEM and SecondSol search, so behavior-changing superiority is not established.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Poland's large installed base and the cited 10-15-year inverter life support a growing replacement need, while documentation requirements make competent handling valuable. Countervailing forces include fast OEM repowering, mature incumbent supply, cheap new hardware in some categories, and incomplete second-life assurance practices.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: The family installer offers unusually credible access to initial cases, and recurring installer accounts are a focused B2B route compatible with the founder's profile. No evidence yet shows technicians will submit cases, share outcomes, pay the desk, or adopt it repeatedly, and repeatable acquisition beyond the family channel is undefined.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder's data and automation skills fit intake, routing, and case-graph development, and the stated capital and time are plausible for a bounded pilot if partners own physical operations. Execution still hinges on qualified partners, fragmented compatibility, item-level compliance, returns, safety, guarantees, and careful allocation of product-liability risk.

highest_value_structural_change: Replace the pure residual-case success-fee model with a contracted installer portfolio service: charge a modest recurring fee for triage, OEM and marketplace routing, and documentation across all submitted cases, plus a success fee for difficult resolutions, with annual case minimums and tightly bounded guarantees. This would reduce adverse selection, monetize the broader workflow, improve revenue predictability, and accelerate the case graph, but should be adopted only if pilots demonstrate willingness to pay.
main_structural_strength: A capital-light, installer-facing resolution workflow can start with real family-installer cases, use existing OEM and marketplace supply rather than fund inventory, and potentially compound verified fitment outcomes into a useful local data asset.
primary_score_limiter: The packet does not quantify how many economically valuable cases remain after OEM and SecondSol channels, nor whether those unusually difficult cases can be resolved repeatedly at positive contribution and sufficient account-level frequency to create scalable owner earnings.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: SecondSol already offers the near-exact marketplace, testing, repair, logistics, and spare-parts stack to more than 60000 users, while OEM replacement can resolve technically substitutable failures quickly; this directly compresses the candidate into a small, fragmented, and potentially adverse-selected remainder.
